questions.stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) has damage to the myelin sheath around their neurones. What effect would this have on nerve impulse transmission?

options.text: Impulses would travel faster because there is less insulation
Impulses would travel more slowly or fail to transmit, because the myelin sheath normally speeds up impulse conduction
Impulses would become stronger due to reduced insulation
There would be no effect because the myelin sheath has no role in conduction

questions.explanation: The myelin sheath is a fatty layer that insulates the axon and allows nerve impulses to 'jump' between gaps (nodes of Ranvier) in saltatory conduction, greatly increasing speed. Damage to myelin (as in MS) slows or blocks impulse transmission, causing symptoms like numbness and muscle weakness.

questions.stem: Under a microscope, a student identifies a neurone with a long axon, a cell body at one end, and dendrites at the other. The axon connects to a muscle. What type of neurone is this?

options.text: Sensory neurone — it carries impulses from receptors
Relay neurone — it connects neurones within the CNS
Motor neurone — it carries impulses from the CNS to an effector (muscle)
Receptor cell — it detects stimuli

questions.explanation: Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands). They have a cell body at one end (within or near the CNS), a long axon, and motor end plates connecting to muscles. Sensory neurones have the cell body along the middle of the axon.

questions.stem: Sensory neurones have their cell body located along the length of the axon, rather than at one end. A student asks why the three types of neurone have different structures. What is the best explanation?

options.text: All neurones are identical in structure; the differences are an artefact of microscopy
Each type is adapted to its specific function — sensory neurones transmit from receptors to CNS, relay neurones connect within the CNS, and motor neurones transmit from CNS to effectors
The differences are due to the neurones being at different stages of development
Only motor neurones are true neurones; the others are supporting cells

questions.explanation: The structural differences between neurone types reflect their different functions and positions in the nervous pathway. Sensory neurones are adapted to receive and transmit signals from receptors, relay neurones connect within the CNS, and motor neurones have long axons to reach distant effectors.

questions.stem: A neurone has many short extensions (dendrites) branching from the cell body. What is the function of these dendrites?

options.text: To insulate the axon and speed up impulse transmission
To receive impulses from other neurones or receptor cells and pass them to the cell body
To release neurotransmitters into the synapse
To produce myelin for the axon

questions.explanation: Dendrites are short, branching extensions that increase the surface area for receiving signals. They pick up impulses from other neurones (across synapses) or from receptor cells and channel them towards the cell body, which then passes the impulse along the axon.

questions.stem: Some neurones in the leg can be up to 1 metre long. What structural feature allows these neurones to transmit impulses rapidly over such long distances?

options.text: They have very large cell bodies that generate stronger impulses
They have long myelinated axons with nodes of Ranvier, enabling fast saltatory conduction
They have more mitochondria than any other cell in the body
They divide into multiple shorter neurones to cover the distance

questions.explanation: Long neurones have myelinated axons. The myelin sheath acts as an insulator, and impulses jump between the gaps (nodes of Ranvier) in a process called saltatory conduction. This is much faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon.
